items.stem: A 49-year-old woman who had a gastric bypass nine years ago develops progressive imbalance, numb feet, and a stiff, spastic gait. Examination shows impaired vibration and position sense in the legs, brisk knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Blood counts show anemia and neutropenia, and her vitamin B12 level is normal. Which deficiency is most likely responsible?
items.explanation: Copper deficiency after bariatric surgery or excess zinc intake causes a myeloneuropathy that mimics subacute combined degeneration, with posterior column dysfunction, spasticity, anemia, and neutropenia. The normal B12 level argues against cobalamin deficiency. Vitamin E deficiency causes a spinocerebellar syndrome with areflexia and no cytopenias. Thiamine deficiency causes a painful axonal neuropathy or Wernicke syndrome rather than a spastic myelopathy with blood count changes.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has morning myoclonic jerks that make her drop her breakfast, plus two generalized tonic-clonic seizures after sleep deprivation. Electroencephalography shows 4 to 6 Hz generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges. She wants to remain on treatment through her childbearing years. Which agent is the most appropriate long-term choice?
items.explanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy needs a broad-spectrum drug. Levetiracetam controls myoclonic and tonic-clonic seizures without the major teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate, which is therefore avoided in people who may become pregnant despite its efficacy. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers that can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized syndromes. Lamotrigine is an alternative but may worsen myoclonus in some patients.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman from a country with endemic rheumatic fever has atrial fibrillation and moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. She has just recovered from a cardioembolic stroke affecting the right parietal lobe. Which long-term antithrombotic strategy is preferred?
items.explanation: Atrial fibrillation with moderate to severe mitral stenosis, or a mechanical valve, is valvular atrial fibrillation, for which vitamin K antagonists remain the standard. Trials of direct oral anticoagulants excluded these patients, and in rheumatic disease a direct oral anticoagulant was inferior to warfarin. Dual antiplatelet therapy is far less effective than anticoagulation for cardioembolic prevention.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has two years of clumsiness of the left hand. Her arm is rigid and dystonic and sometimes rises without her intent, and she cannot imitate hand postures. Cortical sensory loss is present in the same arm, and levodopa gave no benefit. Which neuropathologic feature is most characteristic of the usual underlying process?
options: Four-repeat tau deposition in neurons and glia
Three-repeat tau deposition forming Pick bodies
Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
items.explanation: Asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, alien limb, apraxia, and cortical sensory loss form the corticobasal syndrome. Its classic substrate is corticobasal degeneration, a four-repeat tauopathy with ballooned neurons and astrocytic plaques, though Alzheimer pathology can present similarly. Oligodendroglial synuclein defines multiple system atrophy, Pick bodies contain three-repeat tau in frontotemporal dementia, and Lewy bodies mark Parkinson disease.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing transverse myelitis and a recent episode of optic neuritis tests positive for serum aquaporin-4 immunoglobulin G. Which maintenance therapy is approved for her disease?
items.explanation: Aquaporin-4 positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is treated long term with targeted agents: B-cell depletion with inebilizumab or rituximab, IL-6 blockade with satralizumab, or complement inhibition with eculizumab or ravulizumab. Interferon beta, natalizumab, and glatiramer acetate are multiple sclerosis therapies that are ineffective and in some cases worsen neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Eculizumab and ravulizumab are also approved.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with early symptomatic Alzheimer disease starts lecanemab. After the third infusion he has headache and mild confusion, and magnetic resonance imaging shows new sulcal effusions. Which factor most increases his risk of this complication?
options: Concurrent use of a cholinesterase inhibitor
items.explanation: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema are the main safety problem of anti-amyloid antibodies, and risk is highest in apolipoprotein E e4 homozygotes, who also have a higher rate of hemorrhagic changes. Testing is recommended before treatment. Sex and younger age do not raise the risk meaningfully, and cholinesterase inhibitors are commonly combined with these antibodies without increasing the rate of imaging abnormalities.

items.stem: A 5-month-old girl has clusters of flexor spasms. She has several hypopigmented macules on her trunk, and electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia. Echocardiography shows a cardiac rhabdomyoma. Which treatment is the first choice for her seizures?
items.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis presents with hypopigmented macules, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia. Vigabatrin, a gamma-aminobutyric acid transaminase inhibitor, achieves the best spasm control in this setting and is first-line, with visual field surveillance given the risk of retinal toxicity. Carbamazepine can worsen spasms, phenytoin is ineffective, and valproate is a weaker option. Mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitors treat other tuberous sclerosis tumors.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for years. After two weeks of regular ibuprofen for knee pain she develops coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia, and slurred speech. What explains her presentation?
options: Direct serotonergic toxicity from the pain medication and lithium
Reduced renal lithium clearance caused by the anti-inflammatory drug
items.explanation: Lithium is eliminated almost entirely by the kidney, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazides, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors reduce its clearance, raising levels to the toxic range, which causes tremor, gastrointestinal upset, cerebellar signs, and confusion. Lithium is not hepatically metabolized, ibuprofen is not serotonergic, and hypercalcemia is a different long-term effect of the drug. Dehydration and sodium depletion raise lithium levels further.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has had daily episodes of severe right orbital pain with tearing and nasal congestion, each lasting about 45 minutes, for three weeks. Acute treatment with oxygen helps, and verapamil is chosen as a bridging preventive. What should be done before increasing the dose?
options: Obtain a lumbar puncture opening pressure
Obtain an ECG to assess the PR interval
items.explanation: Verapamil is the first-line preventive for cluster headache, but it can cause AV block and bradycardia at the doses needed, so an electrocardiogram is checked at baseline and again after each dose increase. Lithium monitoring would apply only if lithium were used, and opening pressure and sleep testing do not guide verapamil dosing, though sleep apnea is common in cluster headache.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has excessive daytime sleepiness since adolescence, with knee buckling when she laughs and vivid hallucinations at sleep onset. Which therapy treats both the sleepiness and the cataplexy?
items.explanation: This is narcolepsy type 1, caused by loss of hypocretin neurons. Sodium oxybate consolidates nocturnal sleep, reduces cataplexy, and improves sleepiness, and pitolisant has a similar dual role. Modafinil, methylphenidate, and solriamfetol treat wakefulness but have little effect on cataplexy, so they would need an added anticataplectic such as an antidepressant, which venlafaxine can provide if oxybate is unsuitable.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman is admitted with confusion and a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L from a thiazide diuretic. After saline and stopping the drug her sodium reaches 124 mEq/L within 20 hours and urine output is brisk. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue isotonic saline to reach 135 mEq/L overnight
Desmopressin with dextrose to relower sodium
Restrict all fluid intake and observe closely
Give a 3 percent hypertonic saline bolus now
items.explanation: A rise of more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours places a chronically hyponatremic patient at risk of osmotic demyelination, which appears days later as dysarthria, quadriparesis, and pseudobulbar signs from pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis. Brisk water diuresis signals overcorrection, and relowering with desmopressin and dextrose reduces the risk. More saline or hypertonic saline would worsen it, and observation alone leaves the risk.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has lightning-like leg pains, a wide-based stamping gait, and loss of vibration and position sense. His pupils are small, irregular, and constrict to near effort but not to light. Serum treponemal testing is positive. What is the correct treatment?
options: Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin
Intravenous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days
items.explanation: Lightning pains, sensory ataxia, and Argyll Robertson pupils describe tabes dorsalis, a form of neurosyphilis. Treatment is intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10 to 14 days after cerebrospinal fluid confirmation. A single benzathine dose does not reach adequate central nervous system levels, doxycycline is an alternative only in penicillin allergy, and acyclovir treats herpes viruses.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and strikes his chin. He cannot grip a cup, but he can walk with assistance. His arms are markedly weaker than his legs, with a burning sensation in both hands and urinary retention. Which pattern is this?
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury in a spondylotic neck compresses the cord from front and behind, damaging the central gray matter and adjacent tracts, and produces disproportionately severe upper limb weakness with variable sensory loss and bladder dysfunction. Anterior cord syndrome spares only dorsal column function, Brown-Sequard syndrome causes ipsilateral weakness with contralateral pain loss, and posterior cord syndrome produces proprioceptive loss.

items.stem: On examination, a 28-year-old woman has a left pupil larger than the right, reacting poorly to bright light but constricting slowly during near effort. Her left knee reflex is absent. Which test supports the diagnosis?
options: Dilation of the affected pupil to apraclonidine
Failure to constrict to 1 percent pilocarpine
Improvement in ptosis after an ice pack test
items.explanation: A tonic pupil with light-near dissociation and diminished tendon reflexes is Holmes-Adie syndrome. Postganglionic parasympathetic denervation leaves the iris sphincter with cholinergic supersensitivity, so it constricts to dilute pilocarpine that does not affect a normal pupil. Apraclonidine reversal confirms Horner syndrome, failure to constrict to full-strength pilocarpine indicates pharmacologic blockade, and the ice pack test addresses myasthenia.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has a seizure and is found to have a nonenhancing frontal mass with calcification on imaging. Resection shows a diffusely infiltrating glioma with perinuclear halos. Which molecular combination defines the diagnosis?
options: IDH wild-type with TERT promoter mutation
BRAF V600E mutation with CDKN2A loss
items.explanation: Oligodendroglioma is defined by the combination of an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation and codeletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q, a profile linked to better survival and chemotherapy sensitivity. IDH wild-type tumors with TERT promoter mutation behave as glioblastoma, H3 K27M defines diffuse midline glioma, and BRAF V600E is typical of pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma and other low-grade circumscribed tumors.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy develops marked hyperphagia and rapid weight gain after resection of a craniopharyngioma. Which hypothalamic structure was most likely damaged?
items.explanation: The ventromedial hypothalamus is the satiety center, and its lesion, as after surgery for suprasellar tumors, causes hyperphagia and obesity. The lateral hypothalamic area is the feeding center, and a lesion there causes weight loss. The suprachiasmatic nucleus sets circadian rhythm, and the mammillary bodies are linked to memory circuits in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Craniopharyngioma surgery often also causes diabetes insipidus.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has brief arm and facial jerks several times daily, then develops recent memory loss and a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L. Magnetic resonance imaging shows hippocampal T2 hyperintensity. Which treatment is best?
options: Escalating doses of two different antiseizure drugs
Steroids with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Surgical resection of the temporal lobe
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures, limbic encephalitis, and hyponatremia point to anti-LGI1 encephalitis. The seizures respond poorly to antiseizure drugs but quickly to immunotherapy, and early treatment with steroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange improves cognitive outcome. A tumor is less common than with other antibodies, surgery has no role, and acyclovir does not treat an autoimmune process.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has orthostatic lightheadedness, and his supine blood pressure is 165 over 95, falling to 105 over 65 after 3 minutes of standing without a heart rate change. Which medication is most appropriate for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
items.explanation: A large fall in standing blood pressure with a fixed heart rate indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and supine hypertension often coexists. Midodrine, an alpha-1 agonist, and droxidopa raise standing pressure, with the head of the bed raised at night to limit supine hypertension. Propranolol, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide lower blood pressure or volume and would worsen the orthostatic fall.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has had 14 months of slowly progressive weakness of finger extension in the right hand and wrist drop on the left. He has no sensory loss, reflexes are reduced in the weak limbs, and there are occasional cramps. Nerve conduction studies show motor conduction block in the forearm with normal sensory responses. Which treatment is most likely to help?
items.explanation: Asymmetric distal weakness with motor conduction block and preserved sensory studies defines multifocal motor neuropathy, often with anti-GM1 antibodies. Intravenous immunoglobulin is the established therapy. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange, which help chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, are ineffective and steroids may worsen this disorder. Riluzole is used for motor neuron disease, but conduction block and absent sensory involvement make a treatable immune neuropathy the correct diagnosis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought by his friends in continuous generalized convulsions for six minutes. No intravenous access can be obtained, and he weighs 82 kg. Which is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: In status epilepticus without intravenous access, a benzodiazepine by a non-intravenous route is first-line: intramuscular midazolam (10 mg for adults over 40 kg) was shown to work as well as intravenous lorazepam in prehospital use. Phenytoin is absorbed erratically and painfully from muscle and is a second-line agent. Oral levetiracetam is too slow and unsafe during active convulsions, and rectal valproate is not a standard first step.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking an estrogen-containing contraceptive has four days of worsening headache, then a focal seizure. Computed tomography shows a small left temporal hemorrhagic infarct, and magnetic resonance venography shows a filling defect in the left transverse sinus. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation even when venous infarction is hemorrhagic, because the hemorrhage is a consequence of venous outflow obstruction and recanalization reduces it. Warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant follows the initial phase. Antiplatelets are inadequate, and waiting risks propagation. Craniectomy is reserved for refractory herniation, not for a small infarct with a seizure.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease for eight years reports vivid visual hallucinations of children in the room and now becomes agitated at night. He has mild cognitive impairment and has already stopped an anticholinergic and an amantadine tablet. Which antipsychotic is most appropriate?
items.explanation: In Parkinson disease psychosis after offending drugs are removed, treatment with a serotonin 5-HT2A inverse agonist such as pimavanserin, or low-dose quetiapine or clozapine, avoids worsening parkinsonism. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine block dopamine D2 receptors strongly and cause marked motor deterioration, and they are avoided in this population. Pimavanserin needs no blood count monitoring, unlike clozapine.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has a first episode of internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T2 lesions in the periventricular white matter and the pons, with no enhancement and no prior imaging. Cerebrospinal fluid shows unique oligoclonal bands. Does he meet 2017 McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis?
options: No, because a second clinical attack is required
Yes, oligoclonal bands substitute for time dissemination
No, because enhancing lesions must also be present
No, because a follow-up scan after three months is required
items.explanation: Under the 2017 revision of the McDonald criteria, a first clinical attack with objective evidence of lesions in two typical regions (dissemination in space) plus positive cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands establishes dissemination in time, allowing diagnosis without a second attack or follow-up scan. Enhancing lesions are one route to dissemination in time but are not required when oligoclonal bands are present.

items.stem: A 63-year-old retired teacher has two years of word-finding pauses and failure to repeat long sentences. Her speech is slow but grammatical, and single-word comprehension and object knowledge are preserved. Which pathology most often underlies this syndrome?
items.explanation: The logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia is defined by impaired word retrieval and sentence repetition from reduced phonological loop capacity, with spared grammar and single-word comprehension. Most cases reflect Alzheimer pathology. The nonfluent variant is more often tau-related frontotemporal degeneration, and the semantic variant is most often transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 related. Biomarkers of amyloid help confirm the underlying pathology.

items.stem: A term infant has seizures and a poor suck at 4 hours after a difficult delivery with cord-gas pH of 6.9 and an Apgar score of 3 at five minutes. He has moderate encephalopathy. Which neuroprotective treatment is indicated?
options: Cooling to 33.5 degrees Celsius for 72 hours within 6 hours
Cooling to 36 degrees Celsius for 24 hours, started within 24 hours
Hypertonic saline to reduce cerebral edema
items.explanation: Therapeutic hypothermia is the standard of care for term and near-term infants with moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Cooling begins within 6 hours of birth, maintains a core temperature of 33 to 34 degrees Celsius for 72 hours, and reduces death and disability. Mild cooling for a shorter time lacks the proven benefit, and prophylactic anticonvulsants or osmotherapy do not improve outcome.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man taking sertraline is given linezolid for an infection. Within a day he has agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, tremor, inducible ankle clonus, and a temperature of 38.9 degrees Celsius. After stopping the culprit drugs and giving benzodiazepines, which agent can be added if symptoms persist?
items.explanation: Clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, autonomic instability, and diarrhea after combining a serotonergic antidepressant with linezolid, a weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor, are the serotonin syndrome. Treatment is stopping the drugs, sedation, cooling, and, if needed, the 5-HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and haloperidol would worsen the state.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a headache that appears within minutes of standing and resolves after lying down, with neck stiffness and muffled hearing, beginning after a yoga class. Which magnetic resonance imaging finding is most expected?
options: Empty sella with flattening of the posterior globes
Filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus and cortical veins
Diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement with brain sagging
items.explanation: Orthostatic headache with a plausible trigger suggests spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Imaging typically shows diffuse thick pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging, venous engorgement, and subdural collections. An empty sella with flattened globes suggests raised pressure, nodular leptomeningeal enhancement suggests carcinomatous or granulomatous meningitis, and a sinus filling defect suggests venous thrombosis. Treatment starts with fluids and rest, then an epidural blood patch if symptoms persist.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with restless legs syndrome took pramipexole for three years. His symptoms now begin by early afternoon, have spread to his arms, and are more intense. His ferritin is 40 ng/mL. What is the best management?
items.explanation: Earlier onset, spread to other body parts, and greater intensity on a dopamine agonist describe augmentation. Increasing the dopaminergic dose worsens it. Management is to taper the agonist, begin an alpha-2-delta ligand such as gabapentin enacarbil, which is now first-line, and replace iron when ferritin is low (under about 75 ng/mL). Opioids are reserved for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man is found unresponsive in a closed garage with a portable generator running and recovers after oxygen therapy. Three weeks later he develops apathy, memory loss, and parkinsonism. Which imaging finding is most characteristic?
options: Bilateral mesial temporal restricted diffusion changes
Bilateral T2 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus
items.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and inhibits cytochrome oxidase, injuring metabolically vulnerable structures, especially the globus pallidus. Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae with cognitive decline and parkinsonism appear days to weeks after apparent recovery. Mesial temporal restricted diffusion fits herpes encephalitis, cerebellar atrophy fits chronic toxins or degenerative ataxia, and cortical ribboning fits prion disease. Acute treatment is high-flow oxygen, which shortens carboxyhemoglobin half-life.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 30 per microliter has two weeks of headache and low-grade fever. India ink is positive, cryptococcal antigen is elevated, and opening pressure is 38 cm of water. After starting amphotericin and flucytosine, he has persistent headache. What is the next best step?
items.explanation: Raised intracranial pressure is a major cause of morbidity in cryptococcal meningitis, and pressures above 25 cm of water should be lowered by removing cerebrospinal fluid until pressure falls below 20 or by half, repeated daily as needed. Acetazolamide is ineffective and harmful, corticosteroids worsen outcome, and starting antiretroviral therapy too early risks immune reconstitution syndrome, so it is delayed several weeks.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man arrives after a motorcycle collision with a brief loss of consciousness, then lucid interval, then headache and a dilated right pupil. Computed tomography shows a biconvex hyperdense collection. Which vessel is most likely injured?
items.explanation: A lucid interval after head trauma with a lens-shaped hyperdense collection indicates an epidural hematoma, usually from a temporal bone fracture lacerating the middle meningeal artery. Tearing of bridging veins produces a crescent-shaped subdural hematoma, and aneurysm rupture at the anterior communicating artery causes subarachnoid blood. Basilar injury would cause brainstem infarction. Urgent surgical evacuation is required.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations. Her body mass index is 38. Fundus examination shows bilateral papilledema, and magnetic resonance imaging and venography are normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 38 cm of water with normal fluid. Which medication is first line?
items.explanation: Papilledema with normal imaging, elevated opening pressure, and normal cerebrospinal fluid in an obese woman defines idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Weight loss and acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that lowers cerebrospinal fluid production, are first line, with optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting for visual deterioration. Steroids are not recommended, and loop diuretics have little evidence.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 6-week history of headache and a left hemiparesis. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a ring-enhancing frontal lesion with surrounding edema, and biopsy shows palisading necrosis with microvascular proliferation. Which molecular marker predicts a better response to temozolomide?
items.explanation: Necrosis and microvascular proliferation define glioblastoma. Methylation of the MGMT promoter silences a DNA repair enzyme and predicts better response to temozolomide with radiation. EGFR amplification is common but not predictive of response, ATRX loss occurs in IDH-mutant astrocytomas, and the absence of an IDH mutation is the typical wild-type state of glioblastoma and indicates a poorer prognosis.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a lesion that spares the left lower face but causes right arm and leg weakness, with the tongue deviating to the left on protrusion. Which structure is most likely infarcted?
items.explanation: Tongue deviation toward the lesion with contralateral hemiparesis that spares the face localizes to the medial medulla, where the hypoglossal nucleus or fibers and the pyramid lie, commonly from anterior spinal artery occlusion (Dejerine syndrome). Lateral medullary lesions cause Horner syndrome and crossed sensory loss, an internal capsule lesion weakens the face, and a pontine lesion involves different cranial nerves.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has 3 weeks of subacute amnesia, seizures, hyponatremia, and brief arm and face jerks lasting seconds many times daily. Magnetic resonance imaging shows medial temporal hyperintensity. Which antibody is most likely?
options: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) antibody with small cell lung cancer
items.explanation: Subacute limbic encephalitis with hyponatremia and brief faciobrachial dystonic seizures is typical of antibody to leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1, a voltage-gated potassium channel complex antigen. It is usually nonparalytic and responds to immunotherapy. Anti-Hu antibody causes paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis and neuropathy with small cell cancer, anti-Ma2 causes brainstem and limbic encephalitis with testicular tumors, and glycine receptor antibody causes stiff-person spectrum disease.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes has two months of proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Strength improves briefly after sustained effort, and knee reflexes return after a 10-second exercise. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a large increment after exercise. What is the most important next step?
items.explanation: This is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, facilitation of strength and reflexes after exercise, and incremental response on stimulation, caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, usually small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is urgent in a smoker. Thymoma work-up fits myasthenia gravis, edrophonium has little value here, and biopsy does not address the tumor risk.

items.stem: During video-electroencephalography, a 33-year-old man has a seizure with dystonic posturing of the left arm, automatisms of the right hand, and preserved speech. Where is the seizure most likely arising?
items.explanation: In temporal lobe seizures, unilateral dystonic limb posturing lateralizes contralateral to the seizure focus, while hand automatisms occur ipsilaterally. Preserved speech during the event favors the nondominant hemisphere, assuming he is left-hemisphere dominant. Thus left arm dystonia and right hand automatisms point to the right temporal lobe. A left temporal onset would reverse these signs and typically impair speech.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man taking warfarin has a sudden headache and right hemiparesis. Computed tomography shows a 40-mL left putaminal hemorrhage, and the INR is 3.8. Which reversal strategy is best?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K
Fresh frozen plasma with platelet transfusion now
Intravenous vitamin K alone, repeated daily
items.explanation: Warfarin-related intracerebral hemorrhage requires rapid correction of the INR. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate restores clotting factors within minutes and with less volume than plasma, and vitamin K is added to sustain the effect since the concentrate is short-lived. Plasma alone corrects slowly and risks volume overload, vitamin K alone takes hours, and recombinant factor VIIa does not restore all vitamin K dependent factors and raises thrombosis risk.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable for years on haloperidol, develops rhythmic lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and choreiform finger movements that embarrass him. His psychiatrist wants to avoid destabilizing his illness. Which treatment is best?
items.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia from long-term dopamine blockade is treated with vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors, valbenazine or deutetrabenazine, which reduce abnormal movements without worsening psychosis. Anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia, and propranolol treats akathisia rather than orofacial dyskinesia. Raising the antipsychotic dose may mask the movements temporarily but perpetuates the underlying injury. Switching to clozapine is another option when clinically safe.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has taken natalizumab for 34 months and has a positive anti-JC virus antibody index of 3.4. She develops progressive left hemiparesis and word-finding difficulty over three weeks. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a new nonenhancing subcortical T2 lesion. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate stereotactic brain biopsy of the lesion
Repeat serum anti-JC virus antibody testing
Cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR with natalizumab held
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy should be suspected with prolonged natalizumab exposure and a high JC virus antibody index. The drug is held and cerebrospinal fluid is tested for JC virus DNA, which is highly specific and usually avoids biopsy. Corticosteroids are reserved for immune reconstitution syndrome, and repeating the serum antibody adds nothing in a patient already symptomatic.

items.stem: An 83-year-old woman is admitted after hip surgery. On the second night she becomes inattentive, mistakes the nurse for her daughter, and her alertness fluctuates through the day. Vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Scheduled haloperidol until the agitation clears
Lorazepam at bedtime for agitation and sleep
Starting donepezil with rapid dose titration
items.explanation: Acute fluctuating inattention in a hospitalized older adult is delirium, a medical emergency with a reversible cause in many cases: infection, pain, urinary retention, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, and offending drugs. Management is treating causes, reorientation, sleep protection, early mobilization, and vision and hearing aids. Scheduled antipsychotics and benzodiazepines prolong and worsen delirium, and cholinesterase inhibitors do not prevent it.

items.stem: Two siblings carry the same maternally inherited m.3243A>G mitochondrial DNA variant. One has only diabetes and hearing loss, while the other has stroke-like episodes and seizures. Which concept best explains the difference?
options: Heteroplasmy with a tissue threshold effect
Genomic imprinting of the maternal allele
Germline mosaicism for a nuclear gene
items.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA exists in many copies per cell, and mutant and normal copies coexist (heteroplasmy). The proportion of mutant copies varies between tissues and individuals, and disease appears when it exceeds a tissue-specific threshold, so siblings with the same variant can have different phenotypes. Imprinting, repeat expansion, and mosaicism describe nuclear inheritance patterns and do not explain this.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with well-controlled focal epilepsy develops major depression. Which antidepressant should be avoided because it lowers the seizure threshold at higher doses?
items.explanation: Bupropion produces a dose-related seizure risk and is contraindicated in patients with epilepsy or conditions that lower the threshold. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline and escitalopram carry very little seizure risk at therapeutic doses and are preferred first-line agents, and mirtazapine is also acceptable. Depression in epilepsy should be treated, as it worsens seizure control and quality of life.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a continuous strictly right-sided headache for four months with exacerbations of severe pain, ipsilateral tearing, and ptosis. Imaging is normal. Which treatment is expected to produce complete relief?
items.explanation: Continuous unilateral headache with superimposed exacerbations and ipsilateral autonomic features is hemicrania continua, defined by an absolute response to indomethacin. The indomethacin test establishes the diagnosis, with gastroprotection given for long-term use. Verapamil is a cluster headache preventive, sumatriptan is ineffective in this syndrome, and topiramate is a migraine preventive without an absolute effect here.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has excessive daytime sleepiness for 2 years, with sudden loss of muscle tone in the knees when she laughs, and vivid hallucinations at sleep onset. Polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing is planned. Which result is expected?
options: Mean sleep latency of 14 minutes with no REM periods
Mean latency under 8 minutes with two sleep-onset REM periods
Periodic limb movements with arousals as the only abnormality
items.explanation: Sleepiness with cataplexy and sleep-onset hallucinations suggests narcolepsy type 1. The multiple sleep latency test shows a mean latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep-onset REM periods, and the diagnosis is supported by low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin. A normal latency without REM periods argues against narcolepsy. Apneas indicate sleep apnea, and limb movements alone indicate periodic limb movement disorder.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with chronic malnutrition after bariatric surgery has confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus. Which treatment should be given first?
options: Intravenous glucose infusion before any thiamine is given
items.explanation: Confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia signal Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency, and thiamine must be given parenterally and before or with glucose because glucose can precipitate acute worsening by consuming remaining thiamine. Folate and vitamin B12 are important in other deficiencies but do not treat Wernicke encephalopathy. Delayed treatment risks irreversible Korsakoff amnesia, so empiric treatment should never wait for confirmatory testing.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man with HIV infection, CD4 count of 40 cells per microliter, has headache and a single ring-enhancing lesion in the basal ganglia. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. What is the best next step?
options: Empiric pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with reassessment
Immediate stereotactic biopsy before any treatment is started
items.explanation: Ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with a low CD4 count and positive Toxoplasma serology are most often cerebral toxoplasmosis, treated empirically with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin. Improvement in 10 to 14 days confirms the diagnosis, and biopsy is reserved for nonresponse. Radiation is for lymphoma only after tissue diagnosis, and acyclovir treats herpes simplex encephalitis, which does not form ring lesions in the basal ganglia.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man dives into shallow water and has immediate loss of motor function below the neck, with loss of pain and temperature below the shoulders but preserved vibration and position sense. Which spinal cord syndrome is this?
items.explanation: Flexion injury or anterior spinal artery compromise damages the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts while sparing the dorsal columns, producing paralysis with loss of pain and temperature and preserved vibration and position sense. Central cord syndrome causes greater arm than leg weakness, Brown-Sequard causes ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain loss, and posterior cord syndrome causes proprioceptive loss alone.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has sudden vertigo for 3 days with nausea, a left-beating nystagmus that does not change direction. The head impulse test is abnormal on the right, and there is no skew deviation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Posterior circulation stroke involving the cerebellum
Acute vestibular neuritis of the right ear
items.explanation: A unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, an abnormal head impulse test toward the affected ear, and no skew deviation indicate a peripheral vestibular lesion, as in vestibular neuritis. A central cause would show normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation. Benign positional vertigo gives brief positional episodes, and Meniere disease causes episodic vertigo with hearing loss and tinnitus lasting hours.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man wakes at night unable to move his legs after a heavy pasta dinner. He is alert, his legs are flaccid and areflexic, and his serum potassium is 2.4 mEq/L. Strength recovers over hours. Which medication reduces the frequency of attacks?
items.explanation: Attacks after a carbohydrate load or rest following exercise, with hypokalemia during weakness, indicate hypokalemic periodic paralysis, usually from CACNA1S or SCN4A mutations. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide reduce attacks, and potassium is given orally during episodes. Mexiletine is used for myotonia, steroids have no role, and carbohydrate loading would trigger attacks.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who started topiramate three weeks ago for epilepsy develops bilateral eye pain, blurred vision, and halos around lights. Examination shows shallow anterior chambers and raised intraocular pressure. What is the best management?
options: Increase the topiramate dose to control seizures
Add acetazolamide and continue topiramate at the same dose
Stop topiramate and refer urgently to ophthalmology
Reassure and review in one month
items.explanation: Topiramate can cause an idiosyncratic acute secondary angle-closure glaucoma with myopia, from ciliary body edema, usually within the first weeks. It requires immediate drug discontinuation and urgent ophthalmologic treatment to reduce pressure and prevent permanent vision loss. Continuing the drug sustains the cause, and delaying care risks blindness. Cycloplegic and pressure-lowering agents are given by the eye specialist.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman becomes drowsy over two hours. She has a bilateral upward gaze palsy, small poorly reactive pupils, and memory loss, and her limb strength is preserved. Imaging shows infarcts in both thalami and the right occipital lobe. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
items.explanation: Top of the basilar syndrome results from an embolus lodging at the basilar apex, which supplies the midbrain, thalami, and both posterior cerebral territories. This explains the vertical gaze palsy, pupillary abnormality, hypersomnolence, amnesia, and occipital infarcts with relatively spared motor tracts. A superior cerebellar or anterior inferior cerebellar occlusion causes cerebellar and lateral brainstem signs, and a middle cerebral occlusion causes cortical hemispheric deficits.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has had a gait disturbance since age 5, with her left foot turning inward by evening and a normal gait on waking. Examination shows mild leg dystonia and brisk knee reflexes, and brain imaging is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Botulinum toxin injection of the calf
Referral for pallidal deep brain stimulation
items.explanation: Childhood-onset dystonia with diurnal fluctuation, worse by evening and better after sleep, suggests dopa-responsive dystonia, often from GCH1 mutations. A low-dose levodopa trial gives a dramatic, sustained response and is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it should be tried in any unexplained childhood dystonia. Trihexyphenidyl and botulinum toxin are second options, and deep brain stimulation is reserved for medically refractory dystonia.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has painful bilateral vision loss over four days. Fundus examination shows marked optic disc swelling, and magnetic resonance imaging shows long segments of optic nerve enhancement extending into the perineural sheath. Which test is most useful next?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands testing alone
Serum MOG antibody, live cell-based assay
items.explanation: Bilateral, severe optic neuritis with prominent disc edema and perineural enhancement is the typical pattern of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease, confirmed by a live cell-based assay, along with aquaporin-4 testing. Oligoclonal bands are often absent in this disease, so they cannot exclude it. Angiotensin-converting enzyme is a poor sarcoidosis test, and anti-Hu is a paraneoplastic antibody not linked to optic neuritis.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has a magnetic gait with small steps, urinary urgency, and mild forgetfulness over eight months. Computed tomography shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. What is the best next step to predict shunt benefit?
options: Large-volume lumbar puncture with gait testing
Lumbar puncture with only opening pressure
Three-month trial of donepezil and memantine
Frontal brain biopsy at the time of ventriculostomy
items.explanation: The triad of gait disturbance, urinary urgency, and cognitive decline with disproportionate ventriculomegaly suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with objective gait testing before and after, or extended drainage, identifies likely shunt responders. A pressure reading alone does not predict benefit, a cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat gait, and biopsy is unnecessary.

items.stem: By 18 months, a toddler who had developed typically through her first birthday has lost purposeful hand use, wrings her hands constantly, and shows slowed head growth. She has also lost her few words and has breath-holding spells. Which gene is most likely affected?
items.explanation: Loss of acquired hand skills and speech, stereotypic hand wringing, and acquired microcephaly after a period of apparently normal early development define classic Rett syndrome, an X-linked dominant disorder usually caused by MECP2 mutations. CDKL5 produces an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with Rett-like features, UBE3A is linked to Angelman syndrome, and SMN1 causes spinal muscular atrophy.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has had 3 weeks of decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiose plans, and reckless spending. He has had depressive episodes before. He has no psychosis. Which is the most appropriate maintenance medication class?
items.explanation: Elevated mood with decreased sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity lasting over a week, with prior depression, indicates bipolar I disorder. Lithium and other mood stabilizers reduce relapse and suicide risk. Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania or rapid cycling, benzodiazepines only sedate without preventing episodes, and stimulants would aggravate manic symptoms, so long-term protection depends on a drug with proven prophylactic effect.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has 4 to 5 days monthly of severe pulsatile left-sided headache with nausea and photophobia, lasting 24 hours untreated. She has had a migraine with aura and is planning pregnancy. Which preventive agent is best avoided?
items.explanation: Valproate carries a high risk of neural tube defects, reduced cognitive outcome in offspring, and other malformations, so it should be avoided in women who may become pregnant. Propranolol, low-dose amitriptyline, and candesartan are options in migraine prevention, though candesartan and other renin-angiotensin drugs are also stopped when pregnancy is confirmed. Preventive choice should consider comorbidities and pregnancy plans.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has an urge to move his legs in the evening that is relieved by walking, with ferritin of 22 ng/mL. He takes no interfering medication. What is the best initial step?
options: Oral iron replacement targeting ferritin above 75 ng/mL
Start a low-dose opioid as the first line long-term treatment
Start long-term pramipexole at escalating doses
items.explanation: Evening urge to move the legs relieved by movement is restless legs syndrome, and low iron stores worsen it. Guidelines advise iron supplementation when ferritin is under 75 ng/mL. Gabapentinoids are preferred over dopamine agonists for long-term use because dopamine agonists can cause augmentation, a worsening of symptoms. Opioids are reserved for refractory disease, and hypnotics do not address the urge itself.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing hyponatremia of 108 mEq/L is treated and her sodium rises to 124 mEq/L in 24 hours. Four days later she develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and flaccid quadriparesis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, more than about 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours, causes osmotic demyelination of the pons, producing delayed dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, and a locked-in state. Hepatic encephalopathy causes asterixis without this timeline, posterior reversible encephalopathy presents with headache, seizures, and visual loss, and Guillain-Barre has areflexia with a different course.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a left foot drop after a long period kneeling. He cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot and has numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which finding best distinguishes this from an L5 radiculopathy?
options: Reduced sensation on the dorsum of the foot
items.explanation: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head affects dorsiflexion, eversion, and toe extension, while inversion, which uses the tibial nerve through tibialis posterior, is spared. An L5 radiculopathy also weakens inversion and hip abduction, from the tibial and gluteal nerves sharing that root. Weak great toe extension and dorsal foot sensory loss occur in both, and the ankle reflex is normally preserved in both.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has episodes of shaking with side-to-side head movements lasting seven minutes, recurring when she is observed. Her eyes remain tightly closed throughout, and she recalls events afterward. Which feature best supports a functional seizure?
options: Sustained eye closure during the event
Elevated serum lactate shortly after the event
items.explanation: Prolonged ictal eye closure, long duration, fluctuating course, memory recall, and side-to-side head movements favor functional seizures over epileptic seizures, in which the eyes are usually open. Lateral tongue biting, onset out of electroencephalographic sleep, and a transient lactate or prolactin rise all favor epileptic events. Video-electroencephalography capturing a typical event without ictal changes confirms it.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with diabetes has a transient left hand weakness and is found to have a 75 percent stenosis of the right middle cerebral artery trunk. He has had no stroke. Which management is best supported by trial evidence?
options: Dual antiplatelet therapy and intensive risk control
Extracranial to intracranial bypass with postoperative aspirin
Long-term warfarin with INR target 2 to 3
items.explanation: For symptomatic high-grade intracranial atherosclerosis, aggressive medical management beat angioplasty with stenting in the stenting versus aggressive medical therapy trial, because periprocedural stroke was high. That management is short-term dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, and lifestyle change. Bypass surgery did not reduce stroke, and warfarin proved no better than aspirin and caused more bleeding.

items.stem: A 15-year-old boy has progressive gait ataxia, absent ankle reflexes, loss of vibration sense, and extensor plantar responses. He has scoliosis and pes cavus, and his father carries no symptoms. Genetic testing confirms a GAA expansion in FXN. Which screening is most important now?
items.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive, caused by GAA repeats reducing frataxin. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the main cause of death and diabetes mellitus develops in many patients, so periodic cardiac assessment and glucose testing are essential. Ceruloplasmin addresses Wilson disease, and very long-chain fatty acids address adrenoleukodystrophy, neither of which fits the genetic diagnosis. Whole-body imaging has no role.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a first episode of optic neuritis. Magnetic resonance imaging shows three periventricular lesions, one of which enhances, along with two older nonenhancing lesions. According to the McDonald criteria, what do these findings demonstrate?
options: Dissemination in space only, without dissemination in time
Dissemination in time only, without dissemination in space
Dissemination in space and in time on a single scan
items.explanation: Simultaneous presence of enhancing and nonenhancing lesions on a single scan fulfills dissemination in time, and lesions in periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord regions fulfill dissemination in space. Together with a clinical attack, this supports a diagnosis of relapsing multiple sclerosis without waiting for a second clinical event. Counting only one dimension would underestimate what a single scan with mixed enhancement shows.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has 18 months of progressive short-term memory loss. She repeats questions, gets lost in familiar stores, and now needs help with finances. Cognitive testing shows deficits in delayed recall and orientation. Which finding is most expected on magnetic resonance imaging?
options: Frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy
Atrophy of the medial temporal lobes and hippocampi
Ventricular enlargement with a normal sulcal pattern
items.explanation: Progressive amnesia with disorientation and loss of independence is typical of Alzheimer disease, in which hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy appear early, usually before generalized cortical loss. Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy suggests frontotemporal dementia, and cortical ribboning on diffusion imaging suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Ventricular enlargement without cortical atrophy with gait disturbance and incontinence suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl has café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and a unilateral optic nerve glioma noted on screening imaging. Her father has multiple cutaneous neurofibromas. Which gene is affected?
items.explanation: Café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, optic pathway glioma, and neurofibromas are diagnostic of neurofibromatosis type 1, an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutation of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17 encoding neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor that regulates RAS signaling. NF2 produces bilateral vestibular schwannomas, TSC1 causes tuberous sclerosis with cortical tubers and seizures, and VHL causes hemangioblastomas and renal tumors.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman stabilized on lithium develops coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, and ataxia after starting ibuprofen for knee pain. Which statement best explains her condition?
options: Reduced renal lithium clearance from anti-inflammatory use
Direct toxic effect of ibuprofen on the cerebellum and brainstem
items.explanation: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazide diuretics, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors reduce lithium excretion and raise serum concentrations, causing coarse tremor, gastrointestinal upset, and ataxia, which progress to confusion and seizures. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. Ibuprofen is not directly cerebellotoxic, cerebellitis would be unusual, and serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperthermia rather than this picture.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has attacks of severe unilateral periorbital pain lasting 45 minutes, up to 3 times nightly for 6 weeks, with ipsilateral lacrimation and a restless need to pace. Which acute treatment is most effective?
options: Oral naproxen taken as soon as each attack starts
High-flow oxygen at 12 liters per minute by mask
items.explanation: Brief, intense periorbital attacks with ipsilateral autonomic signs and agitation indicate cluster headache. Inhaled 100 percent oxygen at 12 to 15 liters per minute and subcutaneous sumatriptan abort an attack within minutes. Oral analgesics and oral triptans act too slowly for attacks peaking within 10 minutes, so they are less effective. Verapamil is the preferred preventive agent.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with progressive asymmetric limb weakness and fasciculations has a pathogenic SOD1 variant. She asks how tofersen works. Which statement is correct?
options: It blocks glutamate release at the presynaptic terminal
It is a free radical scavenger that crosses the blood-brain barrier
An antisense oligonucleotide lowering SOD1 messenger RNA
It is an antibody that clears misfolded TDP-43
items.explanation: Tofersen is an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide that degrades SOD1 messenger RNA, reducing toxic SOD1 protein, and it is approved for ALS with a SOD1 mutation. Its effect on neurofilament light chain is clear, though clinical benefit is still being defined. Blockade of glutamate release describes riluzole, free radical scavenging describes edaravone, and TDP-43 antibodies are not available.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy had a prolonged febrile seizure at 7 months and now has frequent seizures triggered by fever and warm baths, with developing ataxia and delayed speech. His seizures worsened after carbamazepine was started. Which medication is most appropriate to add?
options: Phenytoin titrated to higher serum levels
Lamotrigine as the sole added agent
Oxcarbazepine at the maximal tolerated dose
items.explanation: Fever-sensitive prolonged seizures beginning in the first year, later ataxia and cognitive delay, and aggravation by a sodium channel blocker suggest Dravet syndrome, usually from SCN1A mutation. Sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, and oxcarbazepine can worsen seizures. Valproate, clobazam, and stiripentol, with fenfluramine or cannabidiol as additional options, are appropriate treatments, and early diagnosis helps avoid harmful drugs and guides counseling.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban presents 3 hours after sudden right hemiparesis and aphasia. His last dose was 8 hours ago. Imaging shows a left middle cerebral artery occlusion with a small infarct core. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanation: A proximal large vessel occlusion with a small core within the early window warrants endovascular thrombectomy, which is not affected by anticoagulation. Thrombolysis is generally withheld after a direct oral anticoagulant dose within 48 hours unless specific laboratory tests are normal. Dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack, not a disabling occlusion. Delay reduces the chance of recovery.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has 4 years of tremor of the hands at rest and on posture, a shuffling gait, and vivid visual hallucinations that began a year ago. She was recently started on haloperidol for the hallucinations and became rigid and immobile. Which agent is most appropriate for her psychosis?
items.explanation: Parkinson disease psychosis is treated by reducing dopaminergic burden and, when needed, using low-dose quetiapine or clozapine, or pimavanserin, which block little dopamine. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine worsen motor function through dopamine D2 blockade. Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist but is not preferred because of the motor risk. The sudden rigidity after haloperidol shows her sensitivity to antagonists.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has bilateral optic neuritis and a 5-segment longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging is normal. Which test is most likely to be positive?
items.explanation: Optic neuritis plus longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments, with a normal brain, characterizes neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, associated with antibody to aquaporin-4 water channels on astrocytes. Oligoclonal bands appear in most patients with multiple sclerosis but are infrequent here. Myelin basic protein antibodies lack diagnostic value, and GAD65 antibodies are tied to stiff-person syndrome.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has 2 years of personality change with disinhibition, compulsive eating of sweets, and loss of empathy. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively preserved. Which finding is most expected on neuroimaging?
options: Hippocampal atrophy as the dominant finding
items.explanation: Early disinhibition, hyperorality, and apathy with relative preservation of memory characterize behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, with atrophy of frontal and anterior temporal lobes. Posterior atrophy fits posterior cortical atrophy, which causes visuospatial failure. Diffuse white matter change points to vascular cognitive impairment, and hippocampal atrophy as the dominant finding favors Alzheimer disease with amnestic onset.

items.stem: A 3-month-old boy has episodes of sudden flexion of the trunk with arm extension in clusters, and hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography. Examination shows hypopigmented macules. Which medication is preferred first line for this etiology?
items.explanation: Clustered flexor spasms with hypsarrhythmia indicate infantile epileptic spasms, and hypopigmented macules point to tuberous sclerosis. Vigabatrin, a GABA transaminase inhibitor, is first line for spasms from tuberous sclerosis, with the risk of retinal toxicity requiring monitoring. Carbamazepine can worsen spasms, phenobarbital is ineffective, and ethosuximide treats absence seizures without any role in this syndrome.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has episodes of sudden intense fear with palpitations, chest tightness, and a feeling of impending doom that peak within 10 minutes and occur unexpectedly, followed by weeks of worry about another episode. Which is the best long-term treatment?
options: Daily scheduled alprazolam as the primary long-term treatment
Serotonin reuptake inhibitor with cognitive behavioral therapy
items.explanation: Recurrent unexpected attacks with a peak of fear within minutes and persistent concern about recurrence define panic disorder. First-line long-term therapy is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor or cognitive behavioral therapy, which are often combined. Benzodiazepines provide quick relief but cause dependence and are not recommended as primary treatment, beta blockers do not prevent panic, and antipsychotics lack evidence here.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man reports 3 years of cramps, tremulous hands, and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows tongue fasciculations, facial twitching on contraction, breast enlargement, and proximal limb atrophy with diminished reflexes. Sensory nerve action potentials are reduced. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene
GGGGCC repeat expansion in the C9orf72 gene
Deletion of the survival motor neuron 1 gene
Point mutation in the superoxide dismutase 1 gene
items.explanation: Slowly progressive bulbar and proximal weakness with fasciculations, gynecomastia, and sensory involvement in a man defines Kennedy disease, an X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy caused by a CAG expansion in the androgen receptor gene. The C9orf72 and SOD1 mutations cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which lacks endocrine features and sensory loss. Loss of the survival motor neuron gene produces spinal muscular atrophy with childhood onset.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had 3 convulsive events with eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movements, and pelvic thrusting lasting over 5 minutes. She recovers immediately and has no postictal confusion. Serum prolactin is normal. Which test best establishes the diagnosis?
options: Routine awake electroencephalogram with hyperventilation and photic stimulation
Video electroencephalographic monitoring capturing a typical event
Magnetic resonance imaging with epilepsy protocol
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis
items.explanation: Long events with eye closure, asynchronous movements, and rapid recovery suggest functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizures. The gold standard is capturing a typical event on video electroencephalography, which shows no epileptiform discharge. A routine tracing is often normal in both conditions and cannot exclude epilepsy. Imaging and cerebrospinal fluid studies look for structural or inflammatory causes but do not confirm a functional disorder. Prolactin is unreliable alone.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a thunderclap headache followed by transient right arm weakness. Angiography shows multifocal segmental narrowing of intracranial arteries that resolves at 12 weeks. She takes a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
items.explanation: Recurrent thunderclap headache with multifocal arterial narrowing that reverses within about 3 months defines reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, often triggered by serotonergic or vasoactive drugs or the postpartum state. Primary angiitis follows a subacute progressive course with abnormal cerebrospinal fluid and does not reverse spontaneously. Moyamoya shows progressive stenosis of the terminal carotids with collaterals. Giant cell arteritis affects older adults.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has 2 years of irritability, clumsy chorea of the fingers, and impulsive spending. His father died at 55 with a similar illness. Which finding is most expected on brain imaging?
items.explanation: Chorea, psychiatric change, and autosomal dominant inheritance with anticipation indicate Huntington disease, caused by a CAG repeat expansion in huntingtin. Caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns is the characteristic imaging finding. Pulvinar hyperintensity is seen in variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and midbrain tegmental atrophy (hummingbird sign) occurs in progressive supranuclear palsy. Isolated vermian atrophy suggests a spinocerebellar ataxia or toxic cause.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with relapsing multiple sclerosis on natalizumab for 3 years tests positive for anti-JC virus antibody with a high index. Which complication is he most at risk for?
items.explanation: Natalizumab blocks lymphocyte entry into the central nervous system, and risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, caused by JC virus reactivation, rises with positive antibody status, prior immunosuppression, and treatment beyond 2 years. Cryptococcal infection is linked to fingolimod, and fumarate drugs more often cause lymphopenia. Hemorrhagic cystitis is a cyclophosphamide effect. Extended interval dosing and switching therapy are strategies to reduce his risk.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has fluctuating attention, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of children, and acting out of dreams for 5 years. Two months ago he developed mild parkinsonism. What is the best treatment for his cognitive symptoms?
items.explanation: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism define dementia with Lewy bodies. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine improve cognition and psychosis in this disease. Haloperidol can cause severe neuroleptic sensitivity and worsen parkinsonism. Anticholinergics such as benztropine worsen confusion and hallucinations. Memantine has modest evidence and is not preferred as the initial agent.

items.stem: A 14-month-old girl has lost purposeful hand use, developed constant hand-wringing movements, and had deceleration of head growth after normal early development. She has had episodes of breath holding. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Regression of hand skills, stereotypic hand-wringing, acquired microcephaly, and irregular breathing in a girl define Rett syndrome, caused by MECP2 mutation on the X chromosome, usually arising as a new mutation in girls. FMR1 expansion causes fragile X syndrome with macrocephaly and intellectual disability, SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, and UBE3A deficiency causes Angelman syndrome with happy demeanor and ataxia.

items.stem: A 22-year-old student develops a foot drop after sitting cross-legged for an hour, and 2 years earlier had a transient wrist drop after leaning on his elbow. Nerve conduction studies show diffuse mild slowing with focal prolongation at common compression sites. What is the most likely abnormality?
options: Duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17
Mutation of the myelin protein zero gene
Deletion of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17
Mutation of the gap junction beta 1 gene
items.explanation: Recurrent painless mononeuropathies after minor compression, with a family history and diffuse slowing, indicate hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. It results from deletion of PMP22, which leaves myelin vulnerable. Duplication of the same gene produces Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, a length-dependent neuropathy with uniform slowing. Myelin protein zero and connexin 32 mutations cause other inherited neuropathies without episodic compression palsies as the dominant feature.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman taking lamotrigine with stable seizure control starts a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol. Over the following weeks she has breakthrough focal seizures. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Estrogen inhibition of cytochrome P450 3A4 raises lamotrigine levels
Displacement of lamotrigine from albumin binding sites
Estrogen induction of glucuronidation lowers lamotrigine levels
items.explanation: Ethinyl estradiol induces UDP glucuronosyltransferase, which can lower lamotrigine concentrations by about half, so seizures break through. During the pill-free week the level rises and toxicity may occur. Lamotrigine is metabolized by glucuronidation, not mainly by cytochrome P450 3A4. Protein binding displacement and absorption changes are not the established interaction. Monitoring levels and adjusting the dose are recommended.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, left facial numbness, right body numbness to pain, and left Horner syndrome. Where is the lesion?
items.explanation: Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss with contralateral body sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, dysphagia, hoarseness, and vertigo describe the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from posterior inferior cerebellar or vertebral artery occlusion. The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract explain the crossed pattern, and nucleus ambiguus explains the bulbar signs. A pontine basis lesion produces motor deficits, and a midbrain lesion causes oculomotor palsy.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has had gradually worsening dystonia of the right foot for 2 years, with marked fluctuation, being worst in the evening and nearly absent after sleep. A low dose of levodopa produces dramatic and sustained improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary torsion dystonia from the TOR1A mutation
items.explanation: Childhood-onset leg dystonia with diurnal variation and a dramatic, sustained response to small doses of levodopa is dopa-responsive (Segawa) dystonia, most often from autosomal dominant GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiency. TOR1A dystonia does not respond to levodopa. Wilson disease shows hepatic disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and low ceruloplasmin. Tardive dystonia follows dopamine receptor blocker exposure, which she lacks.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has relapsing multiple sclerosis and plans pregnancy in the next year. She is on a drug that requires discontinuation 2 years before conception by accelerated elimination. Which drug is it?
items.explanation: Teriflunomide is teratogenic and persists for months to years because of enterohepatic recirculation, so an accelerated elimination procedure with cholestyramine is used before pregnancy. Glatiramer acetate and interferon beta are compatible with trying to conceive and are generally continued until pregnancy is confirmed or beyond. Dimethyl fumarate is typically stopped before conception, but it clears quickly and needs no elimination protocol.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman has progressive gait difficulty with small steps, urinary urgency, and mild forgetfulness over 8 months. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to cortical atrophy. What is the best predictor of benefit from shunt placement?
options: Dementia as the dominant presenting symptom of the illness
Improvement of gait after a large-volume lumbar puncture
items.explanation: The triad of gait disturbance, urinary urgency, and cognitive slowing with disproportionate ventriculomegaly suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus. A temporary gait improvement after removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, or extended drainage, predicts a good response to ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Gait is the symptom that responds most, while dementia dominance, marked cortical atrophy, and long duration predict poor response.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has 3 years of weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps with difficulty swallowing. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, and cells invading nonnecrotic fibers. Which statement about his condition is correct?
options: It typically responds well to high-dose prednisone
It usually responds poorly to immunosuppressive therapy
It is characterized by a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules
It is usually accompanied by perifascicular atrophy
items.explanation: Selective finger flexor and quadriceps weakness with rimmed vacuoles and invasion of nonnecrotic fibers is characteristic of inclusion body myositis, the most common inflammatory myopathy after age 50. Despite inflammation, it is largely refractory to steroids and immunoglobulin. A heliotrope rash and perifascicular atrophy belong to dermatomyositis, which responds to immunotherapy. Supportive care and dysphagia management are the mainstay.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man has had focal impaired-awareness seizures with an epigastric rising sensation despite adequate trials of levetiracetam and carbamazepine. Magnetic resonance imaging shows left hippocampal atrophy with increased T2 signal. Which is the best next step?
options: Referral to a comprehensive epilepsy center for surgical evaluation
Addition of a third antiseizure medication
Repeat imaging in 12 months before any further decision
Trial of the ketogenic diet under dietitian supervision
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated antiseizure drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance that a third will achieve freedom is low. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the classic surgically remediable lesion, and randomized evidence shows temporal lobectomy gives far better seizure freedom than continued medication. Waiting wastes time and risks sudden death and cognitive decline. Diet therapy is mainly used in children.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man had a transient left eye blackout lasting 4 minutes. Duplex imaging shows 80 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is neurologically normal and expected to live more than 5 years. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Medical therapy alone with annual duplex ultrasound surveillance
Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks plus best medical therapy
Carotid stenting in all cases regardless of age
items.explanation: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70 to 99 percent carries a high early recurrent stroke risk, and endarterectomy performed within about 2 weeks benefits patients with reasonable life expectancy, alongside antiplatelet and statin therapy. Medical therapy alone is inadequate for severe symptomatic disease. Stenting is an option, but it carries higher periprocedural stroke risk in older patients. Bypass surgery has no benefit for extracranial disease.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 6-month history of an unsteady gait, urinary urgency, orthostatic lightheadedness, and a dysarthric speech, with only mild rigidity not helped by levodopa. Examination shows cerebellar ataxia and a supine blood pressure of 150 over 90 falling to 100 over 60 on standing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Idiopathic Parkinson disease with early autonomic failure
Dementia with Lewy bodies with parkinsonism
items.explanation: Early autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary dysfunction) with cerebellar ataxia and poor levodopa response defines multiple system atrophy, which is caused by alpha-synuclein accumulation in oligodendroglia. Idiopathic Parkinson disease usually responds well to levodopa and develops autonomic failure late. Dementia with Lewy bodies leads with cognitive fluctuation and hallucinations. Corticobasal degeneration causes asymmetric apraxia and cortical sensory loss.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis has a 3-day worsening of vision and a flare of leg weakness. Examination confirms a new relapse, and she has no infection. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for 3 to 5 days
Oral prednisone 10 mg daily taken continuously for at least 6 months
items.explanation: Acute disabling relapses of multiple sclerosis speed recovery with high-dose corticosteroids, typically intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for 3 to 5 days, and plasma exchange is used for steroid failures. Low-dose long oral steroids add toxicity without benefit. Cyclophosphamide is rarely used in refractory progressive disease, and an intrathecal baclofen pump treats chronic spasticity but not an acute relapse.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has difficulty releasing her grip on a doorknob, frontal balding, and early cataracts. Her mother had cardiac conduction disease. Electromyography shows waxing and waning discharges. Before general anesthesia, which evaluation is most important?
options: Serum potassium and thyroid function only
Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 hertz to exclude a junction disorder
items.explanation: Grip myotonia, frontal balding, cataracts, and conduction disease indicate myotonic dystrophy type 1, caused by a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK. Cardiac conduction block and arrhythmia, together with sensitivity to respiratory depressants, make electrocardiography and pulmonary assessment essential before anesthesia. Dystrophin staining applies to Duchenne and Becker dystrophy. Repetitive stimulation tests the junction, and electrolytes alone do not address the major perioperative risks.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is found in a convulsion that has lasted 7 minutes, and intravenous access is not yet available. Which is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: Status epilepticus requires immediate benzodiazepine therapy at about 5 minutes. When no intravenous line exists, intramuscular midazolam is as effective as intravenous lorazepam in prehospital trials, and intranasal or rectal alternatives also work. Phenytoin is a second-line agent given only after a benzodiazepine and needs a line. Oral drugs are unsafe with impaired consciousness, and acetaminophen has no role in seizure control.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man develops left neck pain, a partial Horner syndrome, and transient left monocular visual loss two days after a chiropractic neck manipulation. Which finding is most expected on imaging?
options: Berry aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery
Venous sinus thrombosis of the transverse sinus
Crescentic intramural hematoma narrowing the left carotid lumen
Calcified atheromatous plaque at the bifurcation
items.explanation: Neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome and embolic ischemia after neck trauma points to carotid dissection, in which blood tracks into the arterial wall and forms a mural hematoma that narrows the lumen. The sympathetic fibers run along the artery, which explains the oculosympathetic palsy. An aneurysm, venous thrombosis, or atherosclerotic plaque would not produce this combination in a young patient after manipulation.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has repeated eye blinking and throat clearing for 18 months, with brief sniffing and shoulder jerks, preceded by an urge that he can suppress briefly. Tics are mildly bothersome socially. Which is the best initial management?
options: Behavioral therapy such as comprehensive habit reversal
Haloperidol at a moderate dose as the first choice agent
Withdrawal of any stimulant medication and reassurance only
items.explanation: Multiple motor tics and a vocal tic lasting over a year define a chronic tic disorder, and the premonitory urge supports it. Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics is first line for mildly impairing tics. Medication such as alpha agonists or antipsychotics is reserved for those with substantial impairment, and haloperidol is not first choice because of adverse effects. Deep brain stimulation is limited to severe adult cases refractory to other treatment.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis controlled on pyridostigmine is given a course of ciprofloxacin for a urinary infection. Two days later she develops ptosis, dysphagia, and dyspnea. What is the most appropriate explanation?
options: Pyridostigmine toxicity from reduced renal clearance
Development of a coexisting Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Spontaneous thymoma recurrence within two days
items.explanation: Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, and magnesium can impair neuromuscular transmission and precipitate myasthenic crisis. The temporal relation here points to the antibiotic. Cholinergic toxicity would cause miosis, diarrhea, and fasciculations rather than worsening fatigable weakness. A new Lambert-Eaton syndrome does not appear in two days, and thymoma recurrence is not an acute process. Management involves stopping the drug, securing the airway, and giving plasma exchange or immunoglobulin.
